pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–11 years

- **Topic:** Simple Design Problems

- **Standards — UK (DfE Design & Technology KS2, Design):** pupils "use research and develop design criteria to inform the design of innovative, functional, appealing products that are fit for purpose, aimed at particular individuals or groups."

- **Standards — US (NGSS 3-5-ETS1-1):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-1]."

- **Operational details:** The move at this age is from "make something" to DEFINING the problem before making: naming who it is for, what would count as success (criteria), and what limits the work (constraints on materials, time, cost, size). Children learn to phrase a problem so that you could tell whether a solution worked — turning vague wishes ("make it good") into testable criteria ("the cup must hold 200 ml without leaking for one minute") and to distinguish a criterion (a goal the solution must meet) from a constraint (a limit on how you may reach it). Teach with real, bounded briefs and require the criteria to be measurable before any building.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). The child can, given a need, write two or more measurable success criteria and name at least one materials/time/cost constraint, and can sort mixed statements into criteria vs constraints. Not yet expected: formally weighting or trading off competing criteria (that is the next topic).
bestPractices: Start from an authentic, bounded need with a named user ("a younger child needs a way to carry three library books across the playground in the rain") so criteria and constraints have a real referent.
Insist criteria be TESTABLE before any building: rewrite "make it strong" as "holds 500 g without bending" — model the rewrite aloud and have children spot untestable wording.
Explicitly contrast criterion (what success looks like) with constraint (a limit you must work within); use a two-column sort of mixed statements to build the distinction.
Give constraints teeth: a real materials budget / part list / time limit so children feel that a constraint rules options out, not just describes them.
Defer solutions — spend a whole session only defining the problem, so children learn problem-definition is a distinct step, not a preamble to building.
keyRepresentations: Design brief card: NEED / USER / CRITERIA (measurable) / CONSTRAINTS (materials, time, cost) laid out as fillable slots.
A 'testable?' check applied to each criterion — a thumb/tick that only turns green when the statement names a measurable outcome.
Constraint chips (allowed materials, £ budget, minutes) that visibly rule options in or out.
commonMisconceptions: Treating vague wishes as criteria ("make it nice/good/strong") instead of measurable outcomes.
Confusing criteria (goals) with constraints (limits) — e.g. listing 'use only card' as a success criterion.
Jumping straight to a favourite solution and back-filling the problem to fit it.
Thinking there is one 'right' problem statement, rather than a defensible one that makes success checkable.
Ignoring the user — writing criteria for what the maker wants, not what the named user needs.

learn.summary: For learners aged 8–11, teach the shift from 'make something' to DEFINING a design problem before building: name the user, state measurable success criteria, and list real constraints (materials, time, cost, size). The core skills are (1) rewriting vague wishes ('make it good/strong') into testable criteria ('holds 500 g without bending'; 'the cup holds 200 ml without leaking for one minute'), (2) distinguishing a criterion (a goal the solution must meet) from a constraint (a limit on how you may reach it), and (3) keeping in problem-space instead of jumping to a favourite solution. There is no single 'right' brief — a good brief is a defensible one that makes success checkable. The main activity has learners author a full design brief for an authentic, bounded need; supporting activities sort and sharpen individual statements; alternatives use annotated worked briefs and in-role client interviews to elicit and explain these distinctions.

activities.title: Author a design brief for a real, named user
feedback: If a criterion has no checkable condition (e.g. 'make it nice'), prompt: 'How would we CHECK it's nice? What would we see or measure?' and rewrite it together as an observable condition.

If the learner names an object to build before stating need/criteria/constraints, bracket it: 'That might be one answer — but first, what does ANY good answer have to achieve?' Redirect to problem and criteria.
If no limits are listed, ask 'What have we actually got? How long? How much can we spend?' and make listing at least one constraint a required step.
If a constraint is listed as a success goal (e.g. 'use only card' under criteria), point out that this is a limit on HOW you work, not what success looks like, and move it.

If the learner worries there is one 'right' answer, reassure that several different briefs can be valid — what matters is that the need, criteria, and constraints make success checkable, not that they match a fixed solution.

If the reading-corner glare scenario is chosen, test each criterion the same way: e.g. 'How would we check at 2 pm whether the screens are readable?' — by looking at the screens and desk surface, NEVER by looking toward the sun or holding any cover up to the eyes. Also probe 'Could a solution make the corner too dark to read a book?' so a sensible upper limit becomes a criterion too.
activities.rationale: At this age the learning objective is problem-definition as a separate step, so the task must require the child to WRITE a full brief for a named user, not just recognise good wording. Authentic bounded needs give criteria and constraints a real referent, and self-checking against 'could you test a solution with this?' makes measurability concrete.

KS2 pupils use research and develop design criteria to inform the design of functional, appealing products fit for purpose and aimed at particular individuals or groups.
learnerActions: Choose a bounded, authentic need with a named user — for example 'a younger child needs to carry three library books across the playground in the rain', or 'the reading corner gets so bright in the afternoon that children can't read the tablet screens' — and write the NEED in problem terms.

Write at least two SUCCESS CRITERIA, phrased so you could actually check them. For each, ask 'How would we SEE or MEASURE this?' Rewrite 'make it strong' as 'holds 500 g without bending' and 'make it good' as an observable condition.
List at least one real CONSTRAINT on materials, time, or cost (e.g. 'only card and tape', 'one afternoon', 'under £2'), and say what option that constraint rules out.
Spend the whole session only defining the problem — do NOT design or build a solution yet.
Check your own brief: could someone use it to judge whether a finished solution worked? If a criterion can't be checked, rewrite it.
activities.intendedInsight: Defining a problem is itself a distinct act of construction: a good brief turns a vague wish into something whose success you could actually check, names who it is for, and states the limits you must work within — before any building begins. There is no single correct brief, only a defensible one that makes success checkable.

activities.title: Sort statements: criterion or constraint?
feedback: If 'use only card' or a budget is placed under criteria, note it describes a limit on means, not an outcome to achieve.
If a vague goal like 'make it good' is sorted confidently, flag that even as a criterion it isn't yet testable and would need rewriting before it could judge a solution.
activities.rationale: The criterion/constraint distinction is a crisp, judgeable one that a two-column sort builds directly. This supports the main brief-authoring task by isolating one sub-skill, though it exercises sorting rather than full authoring.
sourceClaims: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-1] [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-1].
learnerActions: Take a mixed set of about eight statements (some success goals, some limits on materials/time/cost) and sort each into two columns: CRITERIA (what success looks like) vs CONSTRAINTS (a limit you must work within).
For each placement, say in one sentence why it belongs there — e.g. 'use only card' is a limit on how you work, so it's a constraint.
For any statement you got wrong on a first pass, explain what made it easy to mix up.
activities.intendedInsight: A criterion is a goal the solution must meet; a constraint is a limit on how you may reach it. The same brief needs both, and they play different roles.

activities.title: Make it testable: rewrite vague criteria and set a threshold
feedback: If a rewrite still has no observable/measurable element, ask what you would physically see, weigh, or time to decide success.
If a chosen threshold is unreasonable for the need (far too easy or impossible), ask what the named user actually requires and adjust.
activities.rationale: Turning untestable wording into measurable conditions is the specific skill that makes a brief judgeable. Short targeted rewrites give fast practice; this checks the skill rather than having the child author a whole brief, so pair it with the authoring task.
sourceClaims: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-1] [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-1].
learnerActions: Given a vague criterion such as 'make it strong', rewrite it as a measurable statement (e.g. 'holds 500 g without bending').
Given a need, choose a reasonable success threshold and justify it (e.g. 'the cup must hold 200 ml without leaking for one minute').
Given two phrasings of the same criterion, pick the one you could actually check and say why the other can't be tested.
activities.intendedInsight: A criterion is only useful if someone could observe or measure whether it was met; naming a quantity, time, or observable condition is what makes a wish testable. (The source requires criteria to be 'specified'; making them observable is how we meet that at this age.)

activities.title: Interview the client to sharpen the brief
feedback: If the learner writes criteria for what the maker wants rather than the user, have the client say 'but I need…' to refocus on the named user's need.
If a criterion stays vague after the conversation, have the client ask once more 'how will we test that?' before it is accepted.
activities.rationale: A spoken, responsive interview suits the elicitation side of problem-definition and models the 'how would we know?' habit. On its own it does not require the structured written brief, so use it to feed into the authoring task rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: KS2 pupils use research and develop design criteria to inform the design of functional, appealing products fit for purpose and aimed at particular individuals or groups.
learnerActions: Take on the role of a designer talking to the named user (the 'client') about their need.
Ask the client questions and let the client keep pushing back with 'How would we KNOW it worked?' until each proposed criterion becomes measurable.
After the conversation, write down the agreed need, two or more measurable criteria, and at least one constraint the client named (budget, time, or materials).
activities.intendedInsight: Problem-definition is a questioning stance: good criteria emerge by repeatedly asking how success would be checked and listening to what the user actually needs.

activities.title: Unpack a worked design brief
feedback: If an explanation of 'why measurable' just restates the criterion, press for the specific observation or measurement involved.
If the added criterion is vague or the added constraint doesn't actually rule anything out, send it back for a checkable/limiting rewrite.
activities.rationale: An annotated worked example is good exposition for the criterion/constraint and testable/vague distinctions. Because reading an example does not itself require the child to author or sort their own statements, the added-criterion step is included so it leads into production rather than staying at recognition.
learnerActions: Read a complete, well-formed design brief for a named user (need, user, criteria, constraints).
For each criterion, explain why it is measurable — what you could observe or measure to check it.
For each constraint, explain what option it rules out of the solution space.
Then write one new criterion and one new constraint you think the brief is missing, keeping them testable and real.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing a strong brief dissected shows what 'measurable' and 'limiting' look like concretely, giving a model to imitate when writing your own — and the brief you add to is one defensible version, not the only possible one.

constraints: The main objective is for the child to AUTHOR a brief (need, measurable criteria, constraints) for a named user; sorting tasks and multiple-choice/rewrite exercises check sub-skills but do not substitute for full authoring.
Reading or tapping through a pre-authored annotated brief explains the distinctions but does not require the child to write or sort their own statements; treat it as a model, not the assessment.
An in-role client interview elicits and sharpens criteria but should still end in a written, structured brief; it supplements rather than replaces authoring.
Defer solutions: spend a session only defining the problem so children experience problem-definition as a distinct step, not a preamble to building.
Constraints need teeth — use a real materials list, budget, or time limit so children feel a constraint rules options out, not merely describes them.
There is no single 'right' problem statement; accept any defensible brief whose criteria and constraints make success checkable, rather than marking against one fixed answer.

If the reading-corner glare example is used, any check of light/readability must inspect the screens, desk, or the patch of light on the surface — never ask a child to look at or through a cover toward the sun.
Not yet expected at this level: formally weighting or trading off competing criteria (that belongs to a later topic).

Interactive feedback ideas (e.g. a live 'testable?' indicator that only turns green when a criterion names a measurable outcome; dragging statements into criteria/constraint columns with mis-sorts bouncing back; constraint chips that visibly grey out disallowed items in a mock parts tray) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both cited sources carry verified:false in the source row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source framed a screen-based 'Design Brief Builder' as uniquely 'ideal' and dismissed 3D/spatial media as adding nothing; these catalog-fit claims have been reframed as one proposal with stated affordances and optional interaction examples, not a universal necessity claim.

The diagnostic scenario (afternoon glare on reading-corner tablet screens) and its probe questions are now included as one OPTIONAL example brief within the authoring activity; it is one defensible framing, not the only correct brief, and its observation method is explicitly limited to checking the screens/surface, not looking toward the sun.

probeDeeper: You wrote 'block the light' — how would we check, at 2 pm, whether a solution had done that?
Is there such a thing as blocking TOO much light here? Should that be one of your criteria?
If we only had paper and tape and one afternoon, which of your criteria would be hardest to meet?
assess.correctAnswer: The child states the need in problem terms (reduce glare on the screens in the reading corner), specifies at least two success criteria phrased so you could check them (e.g. 'the screen is readable at 2 pm', 'it doesn't make the corner too dark to read a book'), and identifies real constraints — available materials, time, cost, or that it mustn't block the walkway — all WITHOUT jumping to a particular solution.

errorPatterns.pattern: Jumps straight to a solution instead of defining the problem ('we should just get blinds').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bracket the solution: 'That might be one answer — but first, what does ANY good answer have to achieve?' Redirect to problem and criteria before solutions.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names a specific object to build before stating any need, criteria, or constraints.

errorPatterns.pattern: Criteria are vague and unmeasurable ('make it good', 'make it nice') so you couldn't tell whether a solution worked.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Turn each vague criterion into a test: 'How would we CHECK it's good? What would we see or measure?' Rewrite together as observable conditions.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Success criteria contain no checkable condition — nothing you could observe or measure to decide success.

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits constraints — treats materials, time, and cost as unlimited.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce constraints as part of every design brief: 'What have we actually got? How long? How much can we spend?' Make listing limits a required step.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Lists needs and criteria but names no limits on resources; solution space is treated as boundless.

responseLevels.gap: States a solution rather than a problem, or gives only a vague aim with no checkable criteria and no constraints.
responseLevels.full: Defines the need, gives two or more observable/checkable success criteria, and identifies real constraints — producing a brief against which competing solutions could actually be tested.
responseLevels.partial: Frames the problem and offers criteria or constraints, but the criteria aren't all measurable or the constraints are thin — the brief couldn't yet be used to judge a solution cleanly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The reading corner gets so bright in the afternoon that children can't see the tablet screens. Before anyone builds anything, I want you to define the design problem: write down what need it addresses, at least two things a good solution must do (so we could tell if it worked), and what would limit us — like materials, time, or money. (Set the scenario and watch how the child frames it; do not supply the criteria yourself.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the framing reveals the habit asking can't: a child who understands stays in problem-space and writes checkable criteria, while a child who doesn't leaps straight to 'let's put up a curtain' and never separates the problem from one solution. Whether criteria are measurable only shows when the child writes them down.
